item.title: Reading is a form of active sampling
item.dc:creator: Francesco Donnarumma
item.description: How large language models, eye movements, and active inference meet in a model of reading and dyslexia.
item.content:encoded:
How large language models, eye movements, and active inference meet in a model of reading and dyslexia

Reading can feel so fluent that it is easy to miss how much work the eyes are doing. Each line is sampled through a succession of fixations and saccades. Where we look next is not simply a matter of moving across the page: it shapes the visual evidence available to the reader and, in turn, the interpretation of the text.

In a recent paper with Mirco Frosolone and Giovanni Pezzulo, we asked whether this continuous interplay between linguistic expectations and eye movements can be described within a single computational model. The result is a model that connects large language models, active inference, reading, and a computational hypothesis about dyslexia.

Eyes as hypothesis-testing devices

One useful way of thinking about reading is that the eyes actively test hypotheses. A saccade selects a new location from which to collect evidence. It is therefore an epistemic action: a small experiment intended to reduce the uncertainty that matters for understanding the sentence.

This is the perspective offered by active inference. Instead of separating perception from action, active inference treats both as parts of an ongoing process of inference. The reader forms expectations about the text, samples new visual information, updates those expectations, and chooses where to look next.

The point is not to treat a large language model as a complete theory of human reading. Rather, it provides a computational source of contextual expectations: an explicit model of what the reader may anticipate before the next fixation. Those expectations become useful only when they are coupled to a mechanism for seeking and evaluating sensory evidence.

Known words and unfamiliar words

The same architecture supports two different regimes. When a word is familiar, strong lexical predictions can guide recognition efficiently. When a word is unfamiliar, the system relies more heavily on sublexical evidence, assembling the word syllable by syllable. This echoes the distinction between lexical and nonlexical routes in theories of reading, while keeping both routes within one generative model.

A computational experiment on dyslexia

The model also lets us ask what happens when high-level expectations contribute less effectively to inference. In simulations, attenuating the influence of priors led to more fragmented visual sampling: more, smaller forward saccades and more backward saccades. These patterns qualitatively resemble aspects of eye movements reported in dyslexia.

This does not mean that dyslexia has a single cause, nor that a computational model can replace clinical or educational assessment. It gives us a more precise question to investigate: how could altered confidence in contextual predictions change the way evidence is sampled during reading?

Why bring these pieces together?

Large language models are useful here because they capture rich, context-based regularities in language. Active inference is useful because it specifies how an agent can act on the world to test its predictions. Bringing the two together makes it possible to model reading as an active, embodied process rather than as text processing detached from the eyes that gather the text.

That connection opens experimental questions. Which linguistic predictions should guide the next fixation? When does a reader shift from lexical to syllable-level processing? How do uncertainty and attention affect the balance between moving forward and returning to earlier text? The model is an attempt to make such questions computationally explicit.

The preprint and the code repository are also available.
